#159418. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2444 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the significant whitetail buck and I badly startled each other.
  • Sources indicate that after the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding.
  • But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the significant whitetail buck and I badly startled each other. In the steady rain patter, he apparently didn’t hear me until I’d stillhunted very close to his cedar clump shelter. I almost came unglued when he exploded into view, too spooked to even snort.

Sources indicate that after the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding. So much for my semi-frantic snapshot.

But then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence. Without snow, it took awhile to slowly, alertly follow up. I found the heart-shot buck. That terminal crash noise came from his failing to clear a windfall when the carburetor quit for keeps.

That’s stillhunting at its best. Unlike the prolonged tedium of trail watching or waiting out a drive, stillhunting’s uptight anticipation is an ongoing thrill. When the action does come, it’s often sudden, without warning. Don’t hunt this way if you have a weak heart.

It has been revealed that very old-timers like my 87-year-old father tell me that forest stillhunting was far more common decades ago. Maybe today’s urban hunters don’t trust their stealth and woodcraft skills. Although not an easy way to take woodland game, including elk, the bottom-line reality is that stillhunting can produce game when other tactics cannot.

Obviously, a lone-wolf hunter can’t make drives to himself. Even when sufficient manpower is available, effective drives require thorough knowledge of both the terrain and how local deer use it. If game chooses not to move because it fed well last night, lacks sexual ambition just now or doesn’t like the prevailing weather, trail watching is usually hopeless. For that matter, many mule deer and most elk and moose simply don’t stick that much to established trails.

Industry observers note that the stillhunter is free of such vagaries. Instead of hoping game will come to him, he goes to it — although stillhunting is not the stalking of game already located. Tactically, he has two top priorities. First, to move quietly and alertly, his course basically dictated by wind, terrain and possibly sun direction. Second, to discover game before it sees, hears or smells him. The stillhunter must play a lone-hand game — two hunters seem to make not twice, but four times the noise of one hunter.

Sources indicate that slow movement is a must. A stillhunter covering ground too quickly simply can’t look well enough for concealed game. He also can’t help making extra noise to be picked up by critters who depend on acute hearing every day of their lives to stay out of trouble. They easily detect high frequency noises (including any rustles, squeaks or metallic clinks from our gear and garb) that we often can’t hear.

It has been revealed that the real trick in stillhunting is to do the looking and the moving as two separate functions. If you forget everything else, remember that! When you attempt to look for game and move your feet at the same time, sooner or later you will make unwanted noise — snapping a brittle twig, tripping noisily or whatever.

Recent findings suggest that don’t follow any set rhythm of taking a set number of steps, then stopping. Instead, consider the area that you can see from where you stand as one vision zone. I never move until this zone, of up to 180° ahead and to both sides, has been totally studied.

A vision zone may range out only 50 feet in dense woods or 200-plus yards in more open country. Depending on the extent of the zone, terrain and cover, it may take 30 seconds or several minutes of methodical looking. Often a promising area is worth the time to just sit for extra eyeballing.

It has been revealed that don’t expect to see a full-blown deer or elk looming up ahead like calendar artwork. Look for just parts of the animal as clues. Most forest visuals are vertical lines — tree trunks, etc. An out-of-place horizontal line may be a log or the outline of a deer’s back. A smudge of dull yellow may be autumn leaves or an elk rump. Wide-field binoculars help greatly on such details.

It has been revealed that once, while hunting in the Cascade Mountains, my eye caught a tiny movement ahead. A broad leaf twitching with the breeze? But there was no breeze and, in that evergreen thicket, no deciduous leaves. I waited some minutes, then spotted the movement again for what it was — a blacktail doe’s ear twitching as its owner listened. When she finally moved, right behind her came a shootable buck.

In a recent development, after searching a visual zone (and listening, too), select a route for the next few feet or yards, based on avoidance of brush contact or other potential noise. Footwork is vital. Short steps are quietest. They offer best control of shifting your balance if you ease your foot down and feel a twig likely to snap under full weight. Also, only with short steps can you come down slowly and silently on your toes or the ball of your foot. Long steps force the heel down first, making it much more likely that you will snap twigs or make a soft but tell-tale thud.

Want some expert stillhunting lessons? Simply watch a house cat on the prowl for birds or field mice. Slow movement, long look-listen pauses, obvious patience and great concentration are what make felines the finest stillhunters in nature. Once, in Washington’s mountains, I watched a mountain lion on the prowl. This best-of-all deer hunter resembles a magnified house cat at work.

Sources indicate that big or small, hunting cats are superb at using concealment. You should do likewise. Very often, unseen game ahead will hear you. By moving slowly with minimum noise, you may sound much like just another deer. But the listening quarry will be watching in your direction for visual confirmation. Don’t slow yourself any more than necessary. I use camouflage makeup to make my pale face less visible against dark forest backdrop.

If you can move quietly in some kind of concealment, use that route rather than an easier-looking, more open course. Stick to shadows; avoid sunlit patches. When possible, hunt with the sun behind you. Go over ridgetops with caution, using brush or timber cover. If the hilltop lacks cover, try crawling. Of course, stillhunting must be done into the wind or at least across it — never downwind. Although human sense of smell is pretty pathetic, sometimes the barnyard odor of elk ahead can be detected.

Often a stillhunter has the option of following fresh game tracks. Except under ideal conditions, such as latest snow, one-man tracking demands so much attention that the stillhunter is distracted while he should be looking for actual game. More than once, deer or elk have surprised me, costing me a shot simply because I was distracted by some interesting tracks. If you start trailing, remember that the maker of these tracks may be bedded down somewhere ahead and almost certainly watching his backtrail. To get anywhere close to it will require extremely good stillhunting.

Industry observers note that the lay of the land can be friend or foe. Ridges and hills offer chances to surprise game on the other side. Flat country is tougher because it offers few elevation advantages to the hunter. Although knowing the area always helps, it’s not truly essential for stillhunting. Once, a young stillhunter in our party, fresh to the place, nailed a whitetail buck the second morning. A fast learner, he capped that next year by pussyfooting close enough to a Cascades bull elk to take him with a bow.

The inexperienced stillhunter is often tempted to work mature evergreen timber, where dense shade means little underbrush. But closely spaced conifers self-prune their branches profusely, forming a noisy layer of dead twigs. Such forests can be hunted only when there’s enough wind noise to cover the hunter’s snap-crackle-pop progress. Unless soggy from rain or wet snow, dead leaves are another audio booby trap.

Some timber is open enough to have a good growth of clover or grass, particularly attractive to elk. By contrast, dense coniferous forests contain little ground-level browse to attract feeding game, but they often provide good escape cover when hunting pressure is on. In unseasonably warm weather, the cool shade of thick evergreen timber invites game. In cold weather, the evergreen canopy traps radiant ground heat for considerably warmer bedding than more open forests.

In a recent development, where evergreen timber is lacking, game makes the best of thick brushy cover or tall grasses — the latter is commonly a deer favorite. In real cold or after rain, any warming sun draws game to south or west-facing slopes.

Best time of day for stillhunting depends on several factors. Stillhunting as early as light permits may find game feeding or on the move to bedding. Ground litter then is less noisy, thanks to the night’s dampening dew. But if overnight frost has made fallen leaves ultra-brittle or has crusted the snow, better wait for some midday thawing.

Though rain or a moderate wind helps mask hunter movement sounds, strong winds are a mixed blessing. With their hearing impaired by too much wind, restless animals change location often rather than staying put. That aids the stillhunter, because moving game is far easier to see. But wind-jittery animals, up on their feet and watching for danger they can’t hear, can spot the hunter more readily. Fortunately, a stiff wind covers his extra noise if the stillhunter sticks to thicker cover for extra concealment.

In a recent development, worst of all are those dead-calm Indian summer days, when even your shadow seems to make a racket in the dried-out forest. The only option, then, is to hunt terrain where game can be spotted at a considerable distance (example: from one ridge to another).

Some cover simply can’t be stillhunted. Swampy terrain is impossibly noisy, all the more if there’s any ice to be broken. Dry, fluffy snow can be fairly quiet for walking. But typical autumn snow, heavy and wet, is composed of oversize, many-pointed flakes. Each step compression-shatters untold thousands of such crystalline flakes. That accounts for the appallingly loud squeakiness. Until it’s settled, breaking its flakes in the process, such snow is no good for stillhunting. The settling process may take two or three days unless a thaw speeds it.

It has been revealed that snow characteristics may vary with terrain. North-facing snow is little affected by the weak sun of late autumn, but snow on southern and western slopes settles rapidly with a few hours of sun.

The stillhunter must remember that weather affects game’s likely location. The first serious snowfall often causes deer to hole up in the shelter of thick, low-branching evergreens, where they may stay 48 to 72 hours, believe it or not, even during the rut. Hungry when they finally leave cover, deer then are likely to feed during the day. But until they start moving, the pristine snow will be barren of tracks, leading to the false conclusion that all game has moved out.

In a recent development, of course, game does move out of high country when substantial snowstorms hit. Hunting deer and elk on such vertical migration routes is often considered a trail-watching game. The stillhunter can cover more territory to learn where game is moving — and if it’s moving.

Gear and clothing are critical in stillhunting. Soft leather boots with crepe soles are almost moccasin-quiet but treacherous in steep, wet or rocky terrain. Classic, Maine-style, rubber shoepacs make quiet steps. Their rounded sole edges are not as likely to shear-snap noisy twigs as stiffer, sharp-edged soles do. With any other rubber footwear, wear enough socks to prevent empty space around the foot from audibly pumping air at each step.

Harder, composition soles with lugs are necessary to maintain life and limb in rough country. Alas, such footwear is noisier. The only consolation is that in country steep enough to require lug-soled boots, the stillhunter has a longer “working range” across canyons, etc., and is not quite as vulnerable to making noise as the close-range, flatland hunter. At times, I’ve carried soft sneakers in my daypack to slip on after climbing a ridge that demanded lug-soled, ankle-supportive boots. Another useful trick is to wear a pair of knit leg warmers running from knee-height to ankles. These muffle twig noise and grass swish.

In a recent development, clothing choice is very simple. Whatever the material, it must be soft. Nylon, corduroy and stiff denim are too noisy. Wool and flannel are the great favorites for quiet movement. Some synthetics like orlon and acrylic are almost as good, depending on weave and nap. Rubberized raingear makes less noise than nylon or vinyl. Because a hat’s brim snags noisy branches, wear a cap. Again, wool or knitted acrylic is quietest. I made a simple, woolen pack cover to keep my backpack from imitating a snare drum when I hunker through overhanging branches.

For quiet carrying, a firearm’s barrel length is more critical than weight per se. Although carbines are best, one of my favorite woods rifles has a 24-inch barrel. I find a 26-inch barrel is just too easy to bang against branches. A timber riflescope should have at least a 30-foot field at 100 yards — more would be better, because forest shots are often at close-range game on the run. Yellow shooting glasses contrast brown deer and elk better against evergreen backgrounds.

Sources indicate that pocket hardware like keys, coins and cartridges must be handkerchief-wrapped to eliminate tell-tale clinking. When I rendezvoused with my deer-hunting daughter in the woods, her sardonic greeting was, “Hello, Santa!”.

“Well before I saw you,” she continued, “I could hear you playing ‘Jingle Bells’. What’s in your pockets?”.

A ring of unwrapped keys, that’s what. And deer probably could hear it twice as well as she could.

Although usually not physically taxing, stillhunting is tiring if you do it right. What wears you out is the strain of constant vigilance. And I mean constant! About the time you relax or daydream, up bounds a buck or bull that makes good his escape because you weren’t mentally prepared to react quite fast enough. But if you’re a dedicated hunter, the high-tension hours of stillhunting are memorable whether you score or not.

Sources indicate that this story, “Deer on the Prowl,” appeared in the January 1990 issue of Outdoor Life. Read more from this series:.

If you’re in the market for a trail running shoe, first consider the type of trails you run on regularly: do you tackle rugged, mountainous terrain, or stick to mellow dirt paths? Some trail shoes can handle both adequately, while others are specialized and excel in one or the other. Shoes with smaller lugs are generally better on smoother, firmer terrain, whereas shoes with deeper, more aggressive outsoles are optimized for steep, muddy, or rocky trails. If you like to feel the trail and dance around rocks and roots, you’ll likely prefer a light, more minimal shoe, but if you’d rather let the shoe roll over trail variations, cushioning and protecting while you zone out, you should look for a shoe with a thicker midsole.

According to recent reports, once you’ve narrowed the search to a certain type of trail shoe, you need to find a pair that complements your unique body and stride. Every runner’s body, gait, speed, experience, and ride preferences are different, so every runner will interact differently with each trail shoe. The shoe that your best friend or your sister-in-law loves may be uncomfortable for you and make running feel slow, sluggish, or even painful. Finding the perfect pair of trail running shoes is a seriously personal affair.

The process for choosing the best running shoes is a matter of finding the models that both fit your foot and also feel best when you’re running. To determine fit and feel, there’s no substitute for trying the shoes on and running in them.

According to recent reports, when assessing fit, first pay attention to length. You need room at the end of your toes as your feet lengthen during their dynamic movements on the run. A rule of thumb is to allow a thumb’s width between your longest toe and the end of the shoe. Runners often wear a running shoe a half or full size bigger than their street shoes.

According to recent reports, ensure that the shape of the sole and the upper matches your foot shape. The sole should be as wide or wider than your foot for the whole length, and match the curve of your arch comfortably. The shoe should hold your foot securely over the instep, while allowing the ball of the foot and the toes to splay and flex when you roll forward onto them. Your heel shouldn’t slip when you lift it, and the arch should be able to dome and lengthen naturally. Nothing should bind or rub as you roll through the stride.

It has been revealed that if the shoe fits, it’s time to take them on a short run on a treadmill, around the store, or, ideally, down the block and back. Every trail running shoe has a unique ride created by the type and density of foam in the midsole and the geometry of that foam: its thickness, width, heel-to-toe drop, molded sidewalls or flares, and forefoot flexibility or rocker shape (plus, in an increasing number of models, the presence of and type of embedded plate). Each of these elements interact with each other and your stride to determine how the shoe reacts on landing, how much it cushions, how stably it supports, how smoothly it transitions from landing to toe off, and how rapidly and powerfully it rebounds.

Industry observers note that the best way to choose trail running shoes that complement your body and stride is to find the ones that feel right on the run. Benno Nigg, the world-leading biomechanics professor who proposed this method of shoe selection, calls it the “comfort filter,” but makes clear it is far more than how plush the shoe feels when you step into it. What you want to assess is whether the shoe allows and supports the way your feet want to move, what Nigg calls your “preferred movement path.” In the right shoe, while running at your normal pace, you will touch down where you expect to land, roll smoothly and stably through the stride without noticing the shoe, feel both cushioned from and connected to the ground, and push off naturally, promptly, and powerfully. When this comes together you’ll know that you’ve found your pair.

It has been revealed that it’s likely that several shoes will feel good on your feet. To find the most comfortable, it helps to compare them back to back, like an eye doctor will do with corrective lenses: flipping between “A” or “B,” “1” or “2.” You may also find that different shoes feel better at different paces or level of fatigue, and you may want more than one pair. In fact, research shows that wearing a variety of different shoes is one of the few proven ways to reduce injury risk as it appears to vary the stresses on your feet and joints.

Recent findings suggest that running shoes have long been marketed and sold as prescriptive devices to help runners stay healthy, but there is little scientific evidence correlating shoes, or any specific shoe properties—like cushioning or pronation control—with running injuries. Medical professionals say that it is highly difficult to determine whether a runner needs a certain type of shoe, and studies have shown that prescribing shoes using traditional methods like treadmill gait analyses or wet-foot arch height tests don’t consistently reduce injuries.

Don’t assume that you need more cushioning or more stability if you have sore joints, or if you’re a heavier runner, or if you’re a beginner—evidence doesn’t support many common beliefs. The best way prevent injury is find two or three different pairs that feel right on the run, ease into using them, and vary your shoes, your running surface and your pace regularly (plus avoid rapid increases in your training load and work on improving your mechanics).

Each season, we evaluate upcoming releases from top outdoor brands, distributing samples to testers based on foot shape and local trail conditions and preferences. For this fall update, we evaluated 5 new models alongside 91 previously tested shoes to select the best trail running shoes on the market.

Over two to four months of testing on varied terrain across the country (from Santa Barbara to Boulder, Nebraska to Newly introduced Hampshire), our team provided detailed feedback on fit, comfort, traction, cushioning, and responsiveness. We combined these reports with our own trail testing to select category winners and top recommendations for every type of runner.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a upcoming military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.

In a recent development, the base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest. And ideally it would include 100,000 to 250,000 contiguous acres.

In a recent development, hegseth remarked the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived. He went on to say the best proposals would cut through “the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families.”.

Sources indicate that but much of the “red tape” associated with building a base on hundreds of thousands of acres of unoccupied land is likely federal government red tape. And no clear path at the moment exists for how to requisition and build a new military installation on federal public land, said Mark Squillace, a natural resources law professor at the University of Colorado Law School.

The Department of Defense would need to work around current Bureau of Land Management or U.S. Forest Service management plans that include stipulations for wildlife like migration corridors and winter range closures.

Industry observers note that it’s also unclear if the base needs to support the U.S. Navy, which would limit public-land options since the bulk of the country’s public lands are in the Interior West like Nevada, Idaho and Utah, though the fact sheet notes all locations, even those without water access, are on the table.

The DOD already administers 8.4 million acres in the U.S., but is looking to acquire lands managed by other agencies.

Wyoming, for its part, is eyeing both state and federal land for the base. The state’s adjutant general, Maj. Gen. Greg Porter, told a legislative committee in early November that Wyoming has identified at least four “chunks” of state and federal land, as reported by the Cowboy State Daily last week. Which chunks have not yet been disclosed.

Squillace lined out how building a military base on public land could — or could not — become a reality.

The DOD would first likely need to discuss any public land acquisition with the BLM or Forest Service. If the land use agency agrees that a military base would fit the current land management blueprint, it would need to prepare a draft Environmental Impact Statement that brings up potential complications and confirms compliance with laws like the Endangered Species Act or National Historic Preservation Act.

“A positive review would likely lead to temporary withdrawal of the land from the operation of certain public land laws (like mining and leasing) that could interfere with the operation of the base,” Squillace says, while also noting that existing rights would be protected. Any particularly valuable mining claims would have to be bought out in what he describes as a “time consuming and expensive” process.

Read Next: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

Ultimately, however, Squillace claims any large-scale, long-term use of land would likely need to be approved by Congress, “since such transfers of public land are not authorized under law.”  Whether or not the dramatically different Congress to be sworn in next year would green light a public-land transfer requested by Hegseth also remains uncertain.

But you can scout before hunt days. I scouted the park on Sunday, the day before the first day of hunting on November 16.”.

Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.

It has been revealed that “It was cool and a little windy, but I was seeing deer soon after daybreak,” states Miltroka, a 38-year-old long-haul truck driver from Farmland. “I spotted a good buck far out, but the cover was too thick to shoot.”.

Industry observers note that as the morning wore on, Miltroka got a chance to take two does, and he dropped them both with his Ruger. He toted both does to his truck using a deer cart, since motorized vehicles are not allowed off-road.

The spot was already paying off, and Miltroka had a friend — who had seen a giant deer using the area before the hunt — to thank for tipping him off about it.

“I’d never seen the deer previously, but a buddy showed me a video [he’d taken] of the buck a month earlier while visiting the park … It was a place no one else was hunting, and I checked to make sure it was okay to hunt there – and it was.”.

On the second day of the hunt, Miltroka chose a different tree. He climbed into a big walnut closer to the cover where he’d seen the buck on Monday. But unlike the day before, Miltroka didn’t see much except a coyote. Then, around 8:30, things changed.

According to recent reports, “I heard something raking trees behind me, and I didn’t know what it was. I kept trying to see what was making all that racket, then I saw him out about 70 yards,” he says. “I knew it was a good shooter buck, and when I got him in my scope I squeezed the trigger, fired, and the deer took off running.”.

Miltroka jacked another round into the chamber, but as soon as he picked up the running buck in his scope again, the deer went down.

It wasn’t until Miltroka studied the dead buck through his scope that he realized how immense the deer was.

According to recent reports, “I started shaking, and yelling,” he says. “I got buck fever after it was over … I called a friend of mine and was so excited he asked if I was tied tight to my tree, and I said yes. I was shaking so much I might have fallen out of it.”.

Once he was steady enough, Miltroka climbed down and walked up on the deer.

Industry observers note that “I was in complete shock,” he notes. “I’ve only taken about six bucks, and none even have the size of this one. I was screaming with joy.”.

He filled out a transport tag for his buck, which filled his limit of three deer for the park hunt – only one of which can be a buck. Then he wheeled the buck to his vehicle, loaded it, and drove to park headquarters to check it in.

The buck’s field dressed weight was 181 pounds. The 22-point nontypical was green scored by an official Boone & Crockett measurer the day after Miltroka shot it. It gross scored 227 inches, with a net score of 197 6/8s inches. It has an outside antler spread of nearly 25 inches, and one main beam of the rack measures over 27 inches.

He will have the buck scored again after the required 60-day drying period for B&C and will enter the buck into B&C’s nontypical record category. He’ll also submit his buck to the Hoosier Record Buck Program.

“The park hunts are well run and there are plenty of deer,” claims Miltroka. “I saw lots of deer being checked in during the hunts and some nice bucks.

#159412. I Went Duck Hunting During the Infamous Armistice Day Storm, and Lived to Tell About It

I Went Duck Hunting During the Infamous Armistice Day Storm, and Lived to Tell About It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 glitch of Outdoor Life.
  • There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.
  • It started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 glitch of Outdoor Life.

There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.

It started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60. Fellows went duck hunting in shirt sleeves. The wind picked up velocity as the day went along, but not enough to get excited about — not until late afternoon. Then, with little warning, a full-scale prairie blizzard screamed in out of the northwest.

Industry observers note that by dark the air was smoking with gale-driven snow, and the thermometer plunged near zero. Bitter winds blew all night. The weather experts said afterward that gusts hit 80 miles an hour. The storm laid a track of death and destruction across six states; it pounded ships to pieces on the Great Lakes, blocked roads, isolated towns, paralyzed cities, and buried cars. Hundreds were marooned on highways. A crack streamliner was 27 hours late into Minneapolis. And when the morning of November 12 broke, 20 duck hunters lay dead, frozen in stiff, grotesque poses — scattered on mud bars, sand spits, and willow-grown islands of the Mississippi bottoms between Red Wing, Minnesota, and La Crosse, Wisconsin.

Recent findings suggest that I was among the luckier ones. I spent that terrible night with two companions under an overturned skiff on a mud bar — wet from head to foot, without fire or heavy clothing, pants frozen to my legs, and kept alive only by the body warmth of the men who lay huddled on both sides of me. The storm cost me six weeks of agony in a hospital and half of my left foot. But at least I survived.

It has been revealed that I was 14 at the time, attending high school in my home town of Winona, Minnesota. We got out of classes at 11 o’clock because it was Armistice Day. I scurried for home, planning an afternoon of duck hunting.

According to recent reports, the wind was already fairly fresh and mother was uneasy. “The storm warnings are up,” she told me while getting my lunch. But I grew up in Winona and knew the river, and at that age, bad weather didn’t worry me. The only thing it meant to me was good shooting. Ducks had been scarce all fall and maybe a blow would bring ’em down. So I hurried through lunch, impatient to get in a blind.

While I was loading my gear in the car, my cousin, Bob Stephens, demonstrated up with a partner, Cal Wieczorek, and they decided to join me. Bob was 20, Cal about 19.

We drove to the Prairie Island spillway at the lower end of the Winona pool, where Dad kept his boat. It was a 16-footer, pointed at both ends, with a homemade bracket for an outboard. We decided to hunt a place known as the Firing Line, along the border of the Upper Mississippi Wildlife Refuge, three or four miles upstream. Hunters lined up there to intercept ducks flying in and out of the refuge. In stormy weather the pass-shooting was exceptionally good, and this looked like that kind of day.

The wind was blowing half a gale now and was beginning to bite. Ominous dark clouds raced overhead, and scuds of cold rain pelted down as we clamped our old three-horse outboard on the boat, cranked it up, and headed out into the choppy pool. The three of us were a heavy load, and the skiff made slow headway against the wind.

We didn’t give it a thought then, but we couldn’t have been more poorly prepared. I was wearing cotton clothes — pants, shirt, socks, and a jacket lighter than a hunting coat. I had overshoes over my leather shoes. Bob and Cal were dressed similarly, except for hip boots. Cal and I had gloves. Bob had a heavy raincoat, and I still believe that made the difference between living and dying for me.

We had one book of matches and no pocketknife. I was carrying a 16 gauge single-barrel Winchester; the other two had pumps. Because we intended to pass-shoot, we took no decoys.

According to recent reports, backed up by a series of low dams, the Mississippi is two to three miles wide in that section, flooding its bottoms and forming open lakes, meandering channels, small islands, bars, and rush beds. We threaded our way through this maze, wallowing in the heavy seas. It took us 1½ hours to cover the distance to the Firing Line.

The sky was full of ducks; they were barreling across the bottoms in crazy skeins, riding the wind, and turning and twisting below treetop height. It was plain they didn’t like the weather. Before the afternoon was over I actually swung at a greenhead with my gun as he hovered above my head, almost stationary, while bucking the gale.

Industry observers note that when we finally got to the Firing Line it was too crowded. The blinds were only about 25 yards apart and all occupied. Ducks were rocketing back and forth over the marsh and there was a steady barrage of shooting. We decided to find another spot.

By the time we found it — on a willow-covered island with many rushes in front — we were beginning to lose interest. The wind was howling like a banshee, down off the high bluffs to the west, with sleet and fine snow in its teeth. We hunkered in the willows for almost an hour, killed four ducks, and decided we’d had enough. The cold was already bone-chilling, our hands were so stiff we could hardly handle our guns, and we were starting to worry about getting back to the landing.

Two strangers came by in a little duck boat; they told us they were scared. That settled it for us, but going home was easier noted than done. None of us knew exactly where we were, and when we tried to shove away from shore, the seas threatened to swamp us. We finally dragged the skiff to the lee side and managed to get it afloat and start the motor. But before going 200 yards we ran aground on a mud bar, which we couldn’t skirt because of the wind and seas. We dragged the boat across the bar and started on again.

We did that about four times before finding ourselves by a major open slough and admitting we were lost. It was almost dark now and snowing so hard we couldn’t see 100 feet. We couldn’t even look into the wind — the storm cut our eyeballs like a sandblast. And the slough was a welter of dirty foaming water in which our skiff probably wouldn’t last more than a minute.

In a recent development, while we debated what to do, another boat loomed out of the stormy dusk, riding low with four hunters. Two of them were only a little older than I — one from my home room at school. The others were men who had hunted the river bottoms all their lives. When they stated they knew the way to Prairie Island and could make it without swamping, we decided to follow.

But I couldn’t get the outboard started. Bob and Cal rowed, handicapped by cold-numbed hands, while I tinkered with it. We managed to keep the other boat in sight for a few minutes. Then, pitching and rolling, it disappeared and we didn’t see it again. When our frantic yells brought no answer we realized we were again on our own. It was days before we learned what happened to the other party. Their skiff had capsized when we lost sight of it. Three of the hunters died there, standing in the icy water, not knowing which way to go to dry land. By some miracle one of the boys survived the night and rescue parties found him on a near-by island at daybreak.

Only a few minutes after we lost that boat we were washed ashore on a sand spit. Bob and Cal leaped clear as we grounded and escaped a wetting. I was in the stern of the skiff, working on the outboard — right in the path of a wicked sea that smashed over us the instant we touched bottom.

I can’t describe the shock that icy dunking gave me. I clawed my way out of the swamped boat, and the wind cut like a braided whip. My legs wouldn’t hold me up, so I crawled across the mud until I was beyond reach of the waves and lay there, cold and weak.

Industry observers note that cal and Bob dragged the boat up on dry land, turned it over, and propped one side up to make a shelter. When they finished I crawled under it. My pants and jacket crackled as I moved. They had frozen stiff in the few minutes I lay exposed to the wind.

We still had only a vague idea of our location, but we knew that large open lake, which we couldn’t cross in our puny skiff, lay between us and any landing. We didn’t talk much about it; we didn’t need to. Live or die, we’d have to spend the night where we were.

Recent findings suggest that bob and Cal did everything possible. They gathered rushes and put them under the boat to keep me off the wet mud. Then they searched desperately for firewood, but there wasn’t so much as a scrub willow. They finally found a few pieces of water-logged driftwood, heaped them in a pyramid, and turned the outboard motor up to drain gas on it — a risky thing to do, except in a desperate emergency like ours. But the screaming wind whipped the gas into nowhere as fast as it ran out of the tank. They struck one match after another without getting a spark of fire.

It has been revealed that the last match flared and died in the darkness, and they crawled under the boat and lay down on the wet rushes, one on each side of me. They spread their hunting coats over us and laid Bob’s raincoat on top. The raincoat kept the worst of the wind out and probably saved me from freezing.

It has been revealed that we had little sense of time and hardly talked. Bob told me afterward that I spoke only two or three times during the night, and then I worried about the anxiety my parents must be feeling.

According to recent reports, I shivered for what seemed like hours, with my hands wedged between my thighs, since that seemed to be the warmest place on my body. I prayed silently. I didn’t think much about dying. I believed we’d get through the night somehow and in the morning find our way home. I realized finally that all feeling was gone in my feet; they were wooden stumps, no longer a part of me. I must have dozed, for I recall waking up and feeling warm, but that lasted only a minute or two and then I was shivering again.

The thing I remember best was the unending scream of the wind. It never stopped raging — searching under the overturned boat, wailing, screeching, terribly alive, terribly cold.

Sometime in the night Bob remembered that he had two apples and two sandwiches in his hunting coat. They were frozen hard, but we gnawed at them and they seemed to help.

The sound of distant gunshots reached us several times, and once we thought we heard faint, far-off yells for help. But our own guns were so crusted with ice that we couldn’t fire them, and it was useless to shout.

We knew we weren’t the only hunters lost on the river bottom. Others were enduring the same torture. And we felt sure there must be rescue parties trying to find us, but we didn’t think we could count on them while the storm continued.

Industry observers note that it was days before we learned all that happened that hard night. Rescue efforts began at dark, and men fought the storm and seas all night in skiffs and powerboats. Some even waded the sloughs to bring lost men to shore. It wasn’t a night for small craft, and no one will ever know how many boats were overturned, swamped, and driven back. But the search went on, hour after hour, heedless of the wind, cold, and snow.

According to recent reports, the night was an awful ordeal for the hunters. One party huddled on a marshy island beside a fire started with dead grass and fed with more than 40 cedar decoys. Gas from an outboard was used to rekindle the blaze each time it died down. Another group marched, jumped, and sparred around a fire built from their boats. Still another found a patch of timber, got a fire going, and then shot dead branches off trees for fuel.

It has been revealed that they were the lucky ones; others didn’t fare so well. Two died under an overturned boat, unable to see a bonfire 400 yards away. Two more reached shore along a railroad embankment, crawled halfway up the bank, fell and froze to death, too weak to walk to safety. Others gave up, lay down where they were, without fire or shelter, and died quickly. A few drowned. Most froze. When the last of the living were rescued, the grim search for bodies continued. It was three days before all the missing were accounted for and the final toll of 20 dead was tallied.

In a recent development, toward morning the air cleared enough to let me glimpse lights on the Winona dam, a few miles away. They glimmered through the driving snow, tantalizing and mocking us, but at least we knew now which direction to go when daylight came. About that same time Bob remarked that his hands were frozen and he’d probably lose them. He noted it quietly, as if it didn’t really matter.

It has been revealed that at first light the wind seemed to lose its gale force. It was still blowing hard, but when we studied the lake in the gray light of morning, we decided our skiff might weather the seas.

According to recent reports, we were in bad shape. Cal and Bob could barely stand up; I needed help to get on my feet. Our hands were stiff and useless. The spit where we spent the night was rimmed with a 50-foot belt of ice that made launching our boat a tough job. But we didn’t have much choice. We couldn’t live through the day on that bleak mud bar, and we had no way of knowing when help would come.

Industry observers note that I crawled into the boat. Bob and Cal inched it off the bar, broke a path in the ice to open water, and rowed slowly into the lake. Their hands, however, were too numb for the oars and they lost control when the full force of wind and waves hit us.

Sources indicate that spray froze to the skiff, coating it with ice. My clothes were as stiff as armor, my legs lost all feeling, and I no longer minded the wind. In that condition, with the boat growing ever heavier from its load of ice, we were swept across the Winona pool to the Wisconsin side.

In a recent development, that should have ended things, but there was still more torment ahead. The marsh had frozen and we grounded on the upcoming ice, 100 yards offshore. The ice gouged a big hole in the bow of the skiff, but it wouldn’t bear a man’s weight. Luckily the wind drove us up until the hole was above water, and there we sat with no way to get to shore.

According to recent reports, it was there a search plane found us an hour later. Part of the feverish search that was under way for 50 miles up and down the river, that plane — a Cub trainer piloted by Max Conrad of Winona — had been in the air since shortly after daylight. It was shuttling across the bottoms, spotting lost hunters, empty boats, deserted gear and stranded dogs, and dropping sandwiches, whisky, matches, and cigarettes. It even dipped low enough to shout encouragement to the men as they were found. Nobody in the rescue teams did a better job.

Conrad flew low over us, wagging his wings, and hollered a message we couldn’t understand. Then he was gone, but before long we heard the steady throb of a powerboat and saw the Army Engineers’ launch, Chippewa.

In a recent development, she couldn’t reach us, for we were out of the river channel in shallow water. It took the crew almost an hour to break ice and get to us with a skiff. Before they were through, my dad and a friend of his, who had been looking for us all night, showed up in a powerful outboard. They carried me to the launch, peeled off my shoes and frozen clothing, and for all I was only 14, gave me a man-size slug of whisky. I took it like a man, too, and never knew I’d had it.

It has been revealed that bob spent a week in a Winona hospital, but his frozen hands came through all right. Cal went home that same afternoon. I had a long bout with gangrene and lost part of a foot. I also lost a lot of weight, dropping from 143 to 85 pounds during my recovery. Christmas was less than a week away when I left the hospital, and I guess that was the best Christmas I ever had.

I’m a teacher in La Crosse now and I still hunt ducks on the Mississippi bottoms whenever I get the chance. But, I wear special boots, even on the warmest days, and take along an emergency kit that contains wool socks, gloves, down-filled hat, compass, knife, matches in watertight container, and a small flare gun. I never go without it.

There are too many mistakes in this world to make the same one twice, and any time I’m tempted to be careless, I remember how the wind sounded that awful November night.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

According to recent reports, outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

Industry observers note that and they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

(Photo: Courtesy of Palisades Tahoe).

It has been revealed that california’s ski season is getting an early-season boost in a huge way. A powerful storm system is dumping significant snowfall across the Sierra Nevada, with Lake Tahoe-area ski resorts among the biggest winners.

The storm has delivered some eye-popping totals already. According to resort snow reports from Thursday, Nov. 19, Boreal Mountain picked up 52 inches in the previous 24 hours, while Mt. Rose reported 32 to 36 inches. Sugar Bowl recorded 34 inches, Palisades Tahoe 25 inches, and Kirkwood 27 inches. Northstar and Bear Valley each reported 22 inches.

Recent findings suggest that the snowfall extends beyond Tahoe, too. Mammoth Mountain reported 20 to 32 inches at Main Lodge in the 24 hours leading into Thursday morning, adding to an already promising start to the season.

Recent findings suggest that we’re not jealous here in Colorado. Not at all.

The timing couldn’t be better for resorts gearing up for Thanksgiving week. Several mountains have moved opening dates forward or are preparing to welcome skiers as early as this weekend. Palisades Tahoe, originally scheduled to open Nov. 25, will now spin lifts Saturday, Nov. 21. Northstar, Heavenly, and Boreal are also scheduled to open today (Friday, Nov. 20). Kirkwood just confirmed they’re opening nearly two weeks early, on Monday, Nov. 23.

Industry observers note that but wait, there’s more: Another storm system is expected to move into the Sierra early next week, potentially bringing additional heavy snowfall just in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts are calling for several more feet across the mountains.

Industry observers note that there is one important caveat, fellow skiers: Getting to the mountains could be a challenge. Heavy snowfall has already caused travel disruptions along Interstate 80, and the Sierra Avalanche Center issued a high avalanche danger warning for the Tahoe backcountry. Skiers should check road conditions and resort operations before heading out, and stay out of the backcountry until conditions improve.

This is like an early Christas gift after a disappointing snow season last winter. And with Thanksgiving still several days away, winter is just getting warmed up.

It has been revealed that what do you get someone who loves fishing, but has a ton of gear and is very particular about their rods, reels, and lures? What’s the right gift for someone who wants to start fishing?

In a recent development, I’m a lifelong angler and a gear reviewer so I can help you with both of those scenarios. I put together a list of seven gifts and four stocking stuffers that are guaranteed to make any angler happy. Best of all, they don’t require any special knowledge to buy and start at just $9.

In a recent development, the Victorinox Fisherman is a classic Swiss Army Knife™ designed specifically for anglers. Besides the Fisherman insignia on the side plate, you can tell that this tool was built for  the water by its fish scaler and hook disgorger. Other tools include a large and small knife blade, can opener, 3mm screw driver,  bottle opener, wire stripper, and more. This Swiss-made tool is perfect for throwing in a tackle box or a boat. Besides fishing tasks, this Victorinox will help you with all kinds of everyday jobs. It’s a versatile tool that the angler on your list will use every day. The Fisherman includes a lifetime warranty.

It has been revealed that you’ll notice there aren’t rods, reels, and lures in this gift guide. That’s because they’re too specific to techniques and species to even try to pick the right one. But, one thing that every angler needs is more tackle storage. I promise this isn’t the fishing version of a pair of socks. It doesn’t matter if you’re shopping for someone who deep jigs tuna or flips jigs for bass, everyone who fishes has a never ending fascination with lures. We also genuinely enjoy organizing our beloved lures and appreciate smart designs for carrying them to the dock. That’s why the Bass Pro Shops XPS Backpack is a can’t miss gift.

Industry observers note that author’s Note: This story was originally published in 2020, and Gramps is gone now. After his funeral, we buried his ashes in the woods beneath his stand. A small cross my dad built sits atop the hill where he shot the buck in this story. I think of our hunt that morning, and all of the good times spent hunting and fishing with my grandpa, every time that I pass it.

The boom comes from the southeast, and it’s loud enough to startle me in my treestand. On opening day of deer season in northern Wisconsin, the woods come alive with gunfire: soft pops in the distance, sharp cracks from the neighbors’ properties, and hurried four- or five-shot strings from someone hammering away with a lever gun at deer bounding across a cornfield. But a bang loud enough to reverberate off the tree I’m sitting in? That has to be Grampa’s .300 Win. Mag.

This is my twentieth season hunting our family land—a few hundred acres of mixed timber where we pack in four or five Robinsons each fall weekend to hunt deer. Because there’s limited room to roam, we all have designated stands that change only occasionally from year to year. Gramps has been hunting the same 3 acres for more than a decade.

This deer hunting strategy—sitting in your stand day after day until you kill a deer or the season ends—is the polar ­opposite of the highly mobile trend of tree saddles and cellular trail cameras. Today’s run-and-gun deer hunter must be agile and adaptive, constantly reading conditions and efficiently changing setups. And sure, that style of hunting can be fun and effective. But at our camp, change comes more slowly.

It has been revealed that A few years ago, for example, I tried to get everyone to use trail cameras. While they all agreed it was cool to see pictures of deer and other wildlife, the consensus was that the cameras kind of ruined the magic of it all. My dad noted that if he knew a big buck was out there, then killed a smaller buck, he might feel disappointed. And when I brought a fresh pour-over coffeemaker to camp, I upset the long tradition of our blue enamel percolators, which either take too long to perk or heat too rapidly and boil over. Even though they’re the source of constant bickering each morning, I was ridiculed as some kind of newfangled French barista. ­(Explaining that the pour-over method was invented by a German woman in the 1900s didn’t help my case.).

Two years ago, Gramps shot a small buck with his .300 but didn’t have the gun mounted solidly to his shoulder. The scope slammed into his face and busted his nose so badly he had to check into the ER to stop the bleeding; that summer, my dad and my uncle Pat tried to talk Gramps into shooting a .243 for deer hunting. But on opening weekend Gramps had his major .300 back at camp.

According to recent reports, “Ack, don’t be wimps,” he said, ignoring everyone’s looks of concern. “It’s just a little kick.”.

According to recent reports, ack, don’t be wimps. It’s just a little kick.

You could view this never-change ­attitude as a special kind of stubbornness. Or, more generously, the best kind of perseverance. This is the same attitude that has allowed three generations of Robinsons to master the art of sitting in the woods. That might sound unimpressive because, of course, almost all hunters sit in the woods. But when I got older and started deer hunting with folks outside my family, I noticed subtle differences in how other people hunted. Other deer hunters bring books to read in their blinds or look at their phones to fight boredom. They shuffle around in their seats, sneak naps, and check their watches. Anything to pass the time, like they’re trying to fast-forward the hunt to the good parts. I suspect these are the same people who complain that they’re too busy and that the days fly by too quickly.

But when the Robinsons are deer hunting, we don’t want time to pass. We’re happy to watch a squirrel or a grouse, or just listen to the geese migrate until it’s time for lunch, a buck appears, or the sun sets on the day.

According to recent reports, I’ve had the opportunity to interview some of the best deer hunters in the country, and they’ve shared mountains of tactics and knowledge with me. But I learned the significant lesson, the one that matters most, at our family deer camp as a kid. There’s real value in sitting still, being quiet, and happily waiting for a thing that may never come.

Read Next: The Case for Fresh, Wood-Stocked Deer Hunting Rifles.

It has been revealed that at lunchtime I climb down, fire up my four-wheeler, and drive to Grampa’s stand. My cousin Shawn pulls up at the same time, and we walk toward the voices we hear echoing through the popple. We find my dad, who beat us there, and Gramps standing over a beautiful 10-point with a golf ball-size hole blown through its chest. Gramps tells the story with a look on his face that I can only describe as, “See, told ya.”.

Industry observers note that dad casually mentions that he also killed a buck that morning, so once we get Gramps’ deer to camp, he and I set out to retrieve it. From maybe 80 yards away I can see a massive rack sticking up from the fallen leaves.

“Holy smokes,” I mutter as my dad hoists the antlers of an enormous northwoods 8-pointer. It’s the best buck he’s ever killed, and also the largest buck we’ve ever taken—or even seen—on our land. “He’s a pretty nice one,” he tells me as we lash the buck to his wheeler. “But I didn’t want to take away from Grampa’s massive moment.”.

It has been revealed that by next fall, 80-year-old Gramps will be one year older, and my dad will have major back surgery that limits his hunting for the season. Change will come for the Robinson deer camp whether we like it or not.

Related: This Is How the Boomer Generation Shaped Hunting Culture, for Better and Worse.

In a recent development, but now isn’t the time to worry about any of that. We have to hang the bucks on the meat pole and get the brats ready for lunch. That, after all, is our tradition.

The Rules of Trail Running Etiquette, from the ATRA President

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners.
  • To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other owners.
  • Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the president of the American Trail Running Association (ATRA)—a title that sounds more impressive than it is—and co-author of The Ultimate Guide to Trail Running,” which is now in its third edition, I know a little about the proper behavior of trail runners. And as a six-decade trail veteran myself, I also know a little about the improper behavior of trail runners.

To me, the “rules” of trail running are quite simple and boil down to two principles: respect nature, and respect other owners.

Those two tenets blossom into about 10 “strong suggestions” for sustainable, copasetic trail experiences, but, like with the Golden Rule, it all comes down to showing respect. Here are the basics of what you should know when you hit the trails:.

Close any gates you open, don’t disturb the wildlife or livestock, and respect private land and get permission to enter.

Take only photos and pack out at least as much as you brought in, including gel wrappers. If needed, wear shorts, a jacket, or hydration pack with zip pockets to stow rubbish found on the trail.

Don’t disturb wildlife as frightened animals may be dangerous. Steer clear of trails that disturb sensitive habitats during nesting or mating seasons. When passing horses, use special care and follow directions from the horseback riders. Consider turning around and going another direction when faced with large herds of animals.

In a recent development, don’t play your music loudly, engage in boisterous conversations with your fellow runners (or through speakerphone), or listen to headphones so loudly that you are unaware of your surroundings. Along the same lines, do your social media influencing elsewhere. Nature is not your recording studio. We don’t want to hear you, and you ought to be able to hear others.

According to recent reports, we expect the same of cyclists. This should be obvious but, then again, all of this should be.

As trail runners, we move relatively quickly, especially when we seemingly emerge from nowhere on unsuspecting trail users. This may be alarming, so anticipate and give a courteous and audible announcement of your presence and intention to pass hikers on the trail by stating something along the lines of, “On your left,” or “Trail,” as you approach. Keep an eye out for those wearing headphones, as they won’t hear your warning. Be courteous when passing, slowing down or stopping if necessary to prevent accidental contact. Be ready to yield to all other trail users (cyclists, hikers, horses) even if you have the posted right of way.

In a recent development, this is likely to be controversial, but consider not bringing your dog on group runs and, when you do run with your dogs, be sure to leash them and keep them under your control when necessary to prevent any wildlife disturbances. Be sure to pack out their (and your) waste.

Be cognizant that off-leash dogs often chase wildlife and degrade the outdoor experience of other trail people.

In a recent development, greet and say “Excuse me” to those you see and pass on the trail. This should be a common practice if for no other reason than to alert others to your presence and not frighten anyone. Similarly, be sure to stay in control of your speed, especially when you could cause rocks or other trail features to fall.

Industry observers note that if you startle someone, apologize, and thank them if they’ve stepped aside. A little kindness goes a long way on the trail.

Don’t cut the switchbacks or widen trails by running around puddles,downed trees, or when it is too muddy.

Don’t create your own trails by running off preexisting, well-marked trails. When multiple trails exist, run on the most worn. Stay off closed trails and obey all postings.

Run single file in the middle of a trail, even if it’s laden with a fresh blanket of snow or thick mud. Go over, not around, obstacles like puddles,rocks, or downed tree limbs, as that widens trails, damages vegetation, and causes unnecessary erosion.

In other words, participate in trail maintenance and give back to the trail community.

In a recent development, in a now-infamous Outside opinion piece of seven years ago that went viral, Marc Peruzzi claimed that trail runners are lazy parasites. Ultrarunner and lawyer Stephanie Case wrote a response piece, saying more could be done, agreeing with my stance that “we are guilty as charged … we need [to do] more. A lot more.” Case continued, “Indeed, as trail running continues to increase in popularity, it will become even more vital that we expand our volunteer and conservation efforts.”.

So, carry your weight and do trail work. Volunteer. Go plogging on your local trails.

Sources indicate that technically, those ascending are supposed to have the right of way but, in practice, people often yield to descenders, likely due to speed and momentum. Be polite, maintain control, and be prepared to yield to other consumers, including horseback riders.

Split larger groups into smaller groups as bigger numbers can intimidate other consumers and have a greater environmental impact on trails.

If you come across someone in distress, stop and check whether they need help.

It has been revealed that don’t become a liability by taking risks, getting lost, or ignoring trail closures that require dangerous rescues. Carry proper clothing, nutrition, and hydration so as not to put yourself at risk of exposure. Safety first is always a good rule.

It has been revealed that if running alone, familiarize yourself with the area where you proposal to run and let at least one other person know your intended route. Be prepared for the weather and conditions when you start your run and plan for the worst, given the likely duration of your run. Know and respect your limits and report unsafe conditions and activities to the proper authorities.

It has been revealed that trail running is beautifully simple. So is being a courteous trail runner. Follow these tips for proper etiquette and keep the trails safe, welcoming, and wild!

Breaking: Senate Passes BAAJA, the Massive Permitting Bill That Will Expedite Development on Public Lands

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S.
  • The Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night.
  • Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S. Senate Thursday night and now heads to the House.

The Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night. Support in the Senate eroded over the series of votes, from 73-25 on the first vote Nov. 9 to a final vote of 62-33. A bill requires a simple majority of 51 votes in the Senate to pass.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

BAAJA is co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico often considered a conservation champion, and Sen. Mike Lee, the Utah Republican and architect of recent attempts to sell public land. Heinrich claims BAAJA cuts red tape and will speed up renewable energy projects to help fight climate change, increase jobs, and bring down energy costs for average Americans.

It has been revealed that conservation advocates, however, fear it will also lock in projects many sportsmen and women have spent years fighting, like a copper-sulfide mine by the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the Pebble Mine in Alaska’s Bristol Bay. It also may well open the door for massive data centers on public land, something most of the conservation and sporting community resoundingly oppose.

“I understand this is a substantial, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life earlier this week.

BAAJA proponents say it increases project certainty. Right now, one administration can reverse or cancel permits approved by a prior administration. But by limiting the back and forth between administrations the bill also drastically changes how much oversight a project can receive, even under foundational laws like the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act. The bill will also limit public input into projects and judicial overview.

Many of the nation’s tribes have forcefully spoken out against the bill saying it severely curtails tribal input.

“Overall, the bill, by weakening these bedrock laws, would make it far easier to fast-track AI data centers as well as fossil fuel, mining, and other extractive infrastructure. Once these projects are approved, they would be difficult to unwind,” according to the Western Environmental Law Center. “BAAJA would cause grave, generational harm to the West’s public lands, waters and wildlife, and communities.”.

Heinrich has said he opposes data centers on public land.

“To be clear, BAAJA is federal legislation focused on energy infrastructure and grid connectivity,” a spokesperson told OL in an emailed satement. “It does not ‘permit’ data centers on public lands. State and local government approval is still required. The Senator’s legislation addresses the federal energy infrastructure challenges associated with a grid that cannot keep up with demand; it does not circumvent the state and local processes that determine whether specific projects move forward.”.

Even conservation groups who support portions of the bill question how fast such a massive piece of legislation is moving through Congress. This is the first major permitting reform bill in decades and was introduced Sept. 30.

Read Next: Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Plan Really Means for Outdoorsmen.

According to recent reports, the bill now heads to the House. If representatives make any changes to the Senate version, the Senate must vote again on the bill before it heads to President Trump’s desk for his signature. The president has noted he supports the bill.

This story was updated on Nov. 20 at 2:30 p.m. CST to include comment from Sen. Heinrich’s office.

School Teacher’s First Deer with a Bow Is This 226-Inch Illinois Giant

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago.
  • It has been revealed that “I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life.
  • Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago. As his interest in deer hunting grew, he took special notice of any big bucks he spotted during his daily drives to and from school as a science teacher.

It has been revealed that “I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life. “We don’t use trail cameras. But I got plenty of [phone] photos the last couple years of a really good buck — but only a few photos during the day.”.

Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.

“I had her out in youth season, and she could have taken a lot of does but wanted a buck. One evening we saw a buck, but it was too dark [even though it was still legal light] and Josie didn’t want to shoot in that poor light.”.

Hicks thinks the buck that he and his daughter spotted that evening during the youth season may have been the giant buck he arrowed weeks later.

In a recent development, on Nov. 14 he hung a ladder stand near a wooded thicket full of rubs, scrapes, and plenty of trails. He set the stand for his dad, 77, to hunt during the upcoming Illinois gun opener on Nov. 20.

But that Saturday night Hicks’ wife, Katie, asked her husband if he wanted to bowhunt the stand the next day, before his father got in it the following week.

Hicks said there wasn’t much time that next morning on Sunday before they left for church. Katie said he had a good two hours to hunt from dawn until leaving for church with his family.

She had a good point, Hicks decided, and climbed into the stand the following morning of Nov. 15.

According to recent reports, he sat for about an hour and spotted a doe with twin fawns at 150 yards. Suddenly the doe with young spooked and out stepped the giant buck Hicks had seen from afar for the last two years.

“I was shaking, found my grunt call and blew it once,” he says. “He turned and started walking toward me and my heart was pounding overtime.”.

The buck came steadily closer while Hicks readied for a shot — the first time he would ever draw his bow on a whitetail.

“He walked toward me, stopped, and looked up at me at 15 yards, then he turned to head away,” Hicks notes. “He started through some brush quartering away at 35 yards and I drew, released, and I heard a loud smack.”.

The buck collapsed in his tracks. Hicks’ arrow had hit a bit high, but his 2-blade mechanical struck the spine and the buck didn’t get up.

Sources indicate that hicks managed to wrestle the nontypical out of the woods and, field-dressed, it weighed 187 pounds. His taxidermist aged the buck at 5 1/2 years, with a gross green score of 226 1/8 inches.

Sources indicate that “We all still made it to church that morning,” Hicks claims. “And I even got to teach Sunday School.”.
