Hand cracks are not the ideal terrain for the TX1, but they are just too fun to pass up. (Photo: Anthony Walsh).

There are three things that make an approach shoe “high value:” its price, versatility, and durability. At $159, La Sportiva’s all-new TX1 (replacing the cult-classic TX2) is decently affordable, and was versatile enough to take testers across a range of objectives, including fifth-class ridges in the Sierras and daily crag commutes, and be worn as a slip-on between limit boulder problems. I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

According to recent reports, the breathable upper and shallow dot lugs make the TX1 an excellent shoe for the fair-weather rock climber who dodges rainy forecasts and muddy approaches. Those little lugs provide just enough grip for your average walkoff, but really shine on technical, slabby approaches where surface contact is king. On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

Fit wise, all testers found the TX1 to be comfortable out of the box, thanks to a stock 4mm Ortholite Hybrid insole and a plush Air Mesh lining. (The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

  • Industry observers note that located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow on the mountains above Rollins Pass, Colorado. (Photo: SWKrullImaging via Getty).

A late fall hike turned into an overnight rescue on the Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail on November 14 when a trio of hikers called for a rescue after encountering severe weather and wintry conditions at 11,600 feet.

Industry observers note that located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet. When hiked in its entirety, it also involves 3,742 feet of elevation gain over the course of 18 miles. Recent day-time temperature highs in the area have hovered between 26 and 37 degrees, while lows were recorded at 5 and 9 degrees with wind gusts as high as 50 mph.

Grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR), which responded, noted that the hikers called for help after encountering dangerous trail conditions, significant snow, and navigational struggles. The team dispatched a group of rescuers who rode ATVs up the Rollins Pass Road before dismounting and hiking the remaining distance there. When rescuers made it to the trio, they found the hikers were wet, cold, and tired.

Industry observers note that “The subjects had set up camp but lacked appropriate gear, including fire making supplies, to spend the night in the deteriorating weather,” rescue officials wrote. A second rescue team joined the party later in the evening before accompanying the hikers back to the staged ATVs and from there to the trailhead.

Although most of Grand County has yet to see significant snow, November can be a deceptive time of the year to hike in Colorado’s high country. Trails may appear accessible, but factors like extreme temperatures, inclement weather and reduced daylight hours can make hiking and camping more treacherous than usual.

The Continental Divide Trail is the highest-elevation long trail in the United States, with its high point at the summit of 14,278-foot Grays Peak. Colorado’s section is the highest on the trail; the USFS estimates that the CDT’s average elevation across the state is 10,000 feet.

#159310. Gary Colliver Was a “Big-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (489 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Gary Colliver Was a “Big-Hearted” Climber Who Devoted Decades to Yosemite

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980.
  • Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

Gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In a recent development, in the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

In a recent development, later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a newly introduced route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

To Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions said. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

It has been revealed that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management strategy for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

“There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher noted. Although that initial plan was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

According to recent reports, as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular major wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions noted.

The Garmin CIRQA Is the Health Band for People Who Hate Wearing Watches

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that overview: The Garmin CIRQA is an excellent screenless health band, but it suits people who dislike watches better than current Garmin watch wearers.
  • It has been revealed that I like wearing a massive watch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Recent findings suggest that overview: The Garmin CIRQA is an excellent screenless health band, but it suits people who dislike watches better than current Garmin watch wearers. After more than two months of day-and-night testing, Outside columnist Graham Averill found it tracks sleep, heart rate and HRV, auto-detects workouts and needs charging about once a week, all for $200 with no subscription. The trade-off: you can’t see your data in real time without opening your phone.

It has been revealed that I like wearing a massive watch. Not a fancy watch, but a big, adventure watch with large numbers and all sorts of data on the face like the altitude of my current location and how many steps I’ve taken during the day. I like wearing a big adventure watch because it sends a statement to the world. It notes, “I might be standing in the grocery store checkout line with a shocking amount of ground beef in my cart, but I do cool things in the outdoors.”.

Sources indicate that also, my substantial adventure watch tracks all of my health data. I am a man of a certain age (50), so the world tells me constantly how notable it is to monitor the hours I sleep and my resting heart rate. But Garmin recently released the CIRQA, a newly introduced health band that promises to track every aspect of my life, and it had me wondering if I should ditch the big, ostentatious watch and opt for a more minimalist health band. One without a face. One that sends a different statement to the world, probably along the lines of “please ask me about my meditation practices.”.

So I spent the last two months wearing Garmin’s latest CIRQA health band every day, and I discovered that it is an excellent health tracker that does everything it claims to do. I also discovered that these minimalist health bands aren’t for me. But the CIRQA might be exactly what you’re looking for. Let me explain.

Pros and Cons + Comfortable design + Great battery life + Automatic workout tracking + Awesome sleep score detail + No subscription required – Can’t track data in real time.

I’m all in on Garmin’s ecosystem. I wear the Garmin Fenix 7 watch, I use Garmin’s computers on my bike, and I even track my golf game with Garmin’s app and launch monitor.

As I inch my way closer to death, I’ve become obsessed with knowing every aspect of my health, so I’ve been curious about comprehensive health bands like Whoop. But Whoop is expensive, with an annual subscription that starts at $199. Garmin’s CIRQA promises all of the data of a Whoop without the annual subscription.

So I spent more than two months testing the Garmin CIRQA, wearing it every day and night and charting my health on Garmin’s everything app, Connect.

Industry observers note that the CIRQA tracks all the major data that a health-conscious athlete could want, continuously monitoring your heart rate and heart rate variability (HRV). It tracks your sleep quality, counts your respiration rate and measures your pulse ox and your skin temperature. The smart band then uses all of these metrics to deliver a “Body Battery” score that puts a number on your sleep quality, workout difficulty, and stress levels.

Industry observers note that it’s comfortable and understated. The band is made from a soft, stretchy poly fabric that isn’t waterproof, but dries fast. I wore it on my right wrist most days—I kept my watch on my left wrist—and found it dries fast after a workout, swim or shower. It does as good a job picking up your heart rate as any wrist-based heart rate monitor I’ve tried, and the details about your sleep quality are awesome. You get a Sleep Score every morning, which contributes heavily to your Body Battery score, but you can dig deeper on Garmin’s Connect app to learn how much deep sleep or REM sleep you got, and how many times you were restless and awake throughout the night.

Industry observers note that so far, I’m restless and awake an average of 40 times a night. I think my wife is pinching me in my sleep.

You can also self-report lifestyle choices to the app, like alcoholic beverages and late-night meals or snacks. This option has helped me draw a direct link between booze and poor sleep. I always suspected it—because there’s so much science to back up the theory—but I never wanted to believe it. Unfortunately, you can’t argue with math. A typical sleep score for me is in the high 70s or low 80s. Add a couple of beers toward the end of the night, and that score drops to the 40s.

Yes. I’m impressed with how well the CIRQA automatically picks up an activity. Start walking or hit the gym and the CIRQA tracks every movement, heartbeat and calorie without any prompts or button pushing. If you’ve ever forgotten to click the “start” button before an epic effort, you know that this automatic tracking is awesome. There’s nothing worse than going for a six-mile run that you didn’t track. If you don’t know your total calories burned, did it even happen?

It has been revealed that you’ll get an alert on your phone after the workout that takes you into Garmin’s Connect app, where you can name the activity. The Connect app is a big part of CIRQA’s user interface. That’s where you can get details about each workout or nap, and it’s easy to use. Connect even has a cool coach layer, so you can design workout plans, and it tells you how much sleep you need to get to recover from your day’s effort.

Smart bands like the CIRQA are designed to simplify your health tracking, giving you the data you want to monitor every aspect of your life, but with one less screen to look at—the watch. But you have to open your phone to see any of that health data, which means you can’t dig into your metrics in real time.

Recent findings suggest that I like wearing a watch when I work out because it tracks my heart rate and calories burned in real time. It keeps me honest and has made my workouts more effective.

My Garmin Fenix doesn’t automatically pick up my workouts, and my wife complains that her Apple Watch doesn’t do a good job of that either. The CIRQA’s battery life is great, too. I charge it once a week, about the same as my Garmin Fenix.

Industry observers note that and that’s my takeaway from two months’ of testing the CIRQA: it’s great. The CIRQA does exactly what Garmin says it will do, but it’s not an upgrade from my watch, so I don’t see any reason to switch.

But plenty of people don’t like wearing bulky watches, and many athletes don’t want or need to know their heart rate while they’re working out. If that sounds like you, the CIRQA might be a good option, especially since you won’t be on the hook for a $200 subscription every year.

#159307. Breaking: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2346 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

My alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

Recent findings suggest that I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

It has been revealed that I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and rapidly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

Industry observers note that I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

Industry observers note that as we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

It has been revealed that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

According to recent reports, at that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

Within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Sources indicate that alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

It has been revealed that I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in major walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

Recent findings suggest that the first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we quickly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

It has been revealed that alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

In a recent development, nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

#159305. A Hiker Died Trying to Help His Son After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

A Hiker Died Trying to Help His Son After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (763 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).
  • A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.
  • It has been revealed that the GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow covers the slopes of Southern California's San Gabriel Mountains, where a hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet on Mount Baden-Powell (Photo: Noah Sauve/Getty Images).

A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

It has been revealed that the GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

Industry observers note that “On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside. “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”.

AV Scanner News, a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside‘s request for comment before publication.

It has been revealed that located in Angeles National Forest northeast of Los Angeles, Baden-Powell is a popular warm-weather climb. The standard summit route begins at Vincent Gap, a 6,585-foot mountain pass along Angeles Crest Highway. From there, hikers follow the Pacific Crest Trail for roughly four miles, climbing more than 2,800 feet through 35 wooded switchbacks up the mountain’s north face before reaching an exposed ridge near the summit.

Because the mountain’s north-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, snow tends to linger there, Hazzard told Outside. During warmer days, that snow can melt and refreeze overnight, leaving patches of ice along the trail. Although the San Gabriel Mountains receive snow every winter, the conditions can catch visitors off guard so close to Los Angeles.

Batres had hiked Baden-Powell at least once before, according to the GoFundMe, and Hazzard noted that even experienced hikers face heightened risk once ice forms on the route.

Sources indicate that “If you are experienced and you know the dangers, there’s still a higher risk of something going wrong than there would be without that snow or ice, regardless of how careful you are,” Hazzard noted. “Each winter, we get people going up there who don’t really understand that the hike they did in the summer is now a mountaineering exercise. It’s so steep, and there are dangerous runouts. If you slip, you might hit your head. There’s a lot you can bang into on the way down.”.

It has been revealed that batres’s death occurred just two days after another hiker survived a serious fall on the same mountain. In a November 21 statement on X, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department described rescuing a hiker who had slid more than 300 feet down a snowy chute on Baden-Powell on November 20.

Responders initially struggled to locate the person due to inaccurate GPS coordinates, completing the rescue shortly before worsening weather would have grounded the helicopter.

Similar falls have occurred in past winters. In February 2016, a 69-year-old hiker slid roughly 100 feet down an icy chute before a sheriff’s helicopter airlifted him to a trauma center. Nearby Mount Baldy has also experienced deadly winter accidents, including three hiking fatalities in the first week of January 2026.

In a recent development, despite having climbed Baden-Powell in winter with experienced mountaineers using crampons, Hazzard said he now avoids the peak once snow arrives. Instead, he recommends seeking formal mountaineering training before attempting snow-covered summits or choosing lower-elevation desert trails around Joshua Tree and Palm Springs.

Recent findings suggest that “They shouldn’t do it in the winter,” Hazzard stated. “But winter is the great time to go and do the hikes you can’t safely do in summer, and leave the high peaks alone.”.

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1079 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Zion Draws The Crowds—These 3 Nearby Parks Are Where to Escape Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds.
  • Entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion.
  • Sources indicate that but I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds. (Photo: Arrterra via Getty).

Entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion. With nearly 5 million visitors in 2025, it ranked as the second-most visited national park in the U.S. Once you make it through the entry gate, though, the payoff is real. Visitors walk beneath towering Navajo sandstone cliffs and wade the Virgin River deep into The Narrows. If luck’s on your side, you might even win the permit lottery to hike to Angels Landing.

Sources indicate that but I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape. I was more paranoid than peaceful, constantly stepping aside and watching my footing as I squeezed past other hikers. The incredible beauty of the park draws equally incredible crowds.

According to recent reports, the good news is you don’t have to fight for elbow room to soak in Zion’s beauty. Its neighboring state parks, wildernesses, and national forests get a fraction of the attention, but are just as jaw-dropping. Explore the surrounding Greater Zion region, and you’ll unlock hikes through red rock without the gridlock.

Head beyond Zion for these underrated hiking spots instead.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $15 per vehicle Best for: Hikers seeking desert variety without a grueling trek. Petrified dunes, sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and hikeable lava tubes, all in one park.

Industry observers note that if Snow Canyon State Park were a DJ, it’d spin a killer geological mashup of 180-million-year-old petrified dunes, Jurassic-period sandstone escarpments, and ancient river-carved slot canyons. The drop: cavernous, jet-black lava tubes you can hike into (headlamp recommended). The park packs a huge punch of diverse terrain you rarely see all in one place. It’s especially family-friendly and a good fit for more casual hikers who want photo-worthy views without a grueling trek.

Catch the park’s greatest hits in one go by linking up the Butterfly Trail, Lava Flow Overlook, West Canyon Overlook, and the Petrified Dunes Loop. The roughly 3-mile loop connects the park’s most notable features. Hikers will see ancient lava flows, winding slickrock passages, and sweeping views down into West Canyon. The petrified dunes along the route steal the show. Hikers walk over rolling hills frozen in time while swirling stripes of orange, cream, and crimson dance underfoot.

Looking for more technical hiking? Tackle the trek to Deidre Peak. The 7.4-mile out-and-back climbs nearly 1,500 feet in elevation and requires a Class 3-4 scramble over rugged sandstone outcrops. The trail crosses into the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve, a conservation area protected as a sanctuary for the native Mojave desert tortoise.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle Best for: Hikers and BLM land lovers seeking seclusion and solitude.

Beyond Snow Canyon sprawls Red Cliffs National Conservation Area. The nearly 45,000 acres of BLM land sits within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve at the crossroads of the Mojave Desert, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau. Here you’ll find a mix of plants and wildlife from all three regions. There are two endangered wildflowers that grow only in this corner of Utah: the dwarf bear poppy and Shivwits milkvetch. Both bloom in spring, with peak overlap in late April and early May. Then there’s southern Utah’s classic red sandstone stretching as far as the eye can see.

Popular out-and-back hikes like the 3.5-mile Elephant Arch Trail and 1.6-mile Red Reef Trail show how water and wind erosion turn sandstone landscapes into works of art. Elephant Arch earned its name from a distinct sandstone outcropping that looks uncannily like a trunk, head, and ears. Along the Red Reef Trail, hikers skirt massive, smooth sandstone bowls. These turn into swimming holes during spring rain and monsoon season, which runds July through September.

According to recent reports, the 5-mile Black Gulch and Yellow Knolls Loop drops through a boulder-strewn gulch of dark volcanic rock, then rolls over yellow sandstone knolls. Hikers can also link the Red Reef and Prospector Trails to create a 10.5-mile loop requiring some scrambling and route-finding through remote backcountry canyons. On the return leg, wide views open up to the Pine Valley Mountains in the north, often capped with snow in winter and early spring.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour 15 minutes (Northeast) Entrance fee: None Best for: Hikers looking for trail variety that showcases Utah’s finest terrain.

The state’s largest national forest shows off a completely different side of southern Utah. Dixie National Forest sprawls across nearly 2 million acres, rising from the desert valley around St. George to peaks above 11,000 feet. Sagebrush, pinyon, and juniper give way to aspen groves and conifer forests as you climb. The higher and farther you hike, the more surprises you’ll find: trout-filled mountain lakes, towering hoodoo spires, and the chance to spot Utah prairie dogs in the wild.

In a recent development, dixie gives hikers a taste of the same pink-and-orange Claron limestone that made Bryce Canyon famous. The difference? Here, thick stands of ponderosa pine grow right up against the hoodoos. Plus, the trails see a fraction of the foot traffic, so you’ll have the views practically to yourself.

According to recent reports, if you want more hoodoo action, check out Thunder Mountain Trail. It winds through what feels like a bite-sized Bryce Canyon. The out-and-back trail climbs more than 1,700 feet over 8.6 miles. You’re rewarded with an unforgettable trek through a maze of spires. For an even more awe-inspiring experience, hike early or late in the day, when low sun turns the Claron limestone a vibrant orange.

Looking for a more Zion-esque experience? Ashdown Gorge Trail echoes the Narrows, minus the permits, rental gear, and crowds. It travels 10 miles from the alpine rim of Cedar Breaks to a creek-carved canyon where red rock walls close in overhead. Heads up: There are two popular ways to hike Ashdown Gorge. You can do an out-and-back that starts at the bottom and heads up into the narrows (recommended), or a point-to-point that requires a shuttle.

Industry observers note that for a longer, relatively flat dayhike, opt for the 11-mile Navajo Lake Loop. The trail circles its namesake, peeking in and out of dense pine, fir, and aspen forest, with shoreline views that make it easy to forget you’re in a red rock wonderland.

#159303. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1352 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1352 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Latest York near the Gunks.
  • Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good firm.”.

After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate Latest York near the Gunks. At the moment, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she states of her substantial three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

In a recent development, when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

Industry observers note that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we quickly got all our stuff together.

Industry observers note that we knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

In a recent development, first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

Very quickly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

We got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

It has been revealed that then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

It has been revealed that so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

In a recent development, will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Recent findings suggest that every time we got to a latest belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

According to recent reports, none of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he remarked it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

Sources indicate that we got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

Sources indicate that I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

Sources indicate that it was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a massive light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

According to recent reports, lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Fresh York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

Recent findings suggest that as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

Granite Gear Zippditty Stuffsacks.

As a frequent flier who jet-sets at least once a month and camps three seasons out of the year, I’ve come to rely on “crossover” gear that bridges both worlds. And with how expensive everything has gotten, anything I buy must earn its keep on more than one kind of trip.

Sources indicate that I’ve honed a short list of my favorite gear that comes on most trips I take, from hopping on an international flight to camping with my family for the weekend. These dual-purpose items pack just as easily into a carry-on as they do into a trunk, are versatile enough for city streets and dirt trails, and make sense to use on a long layover and also around the campfire.

I bring these eight items along no matter whether I’m sleeping under the stars or in seat 23B.

Industry observers note that granite Gear is best known for its backpacking and paddling packs, but its most underrated product is the humble Zippditty Stuffsack. I use these zippered pouches for keeping all the little things in order while traveling and adventuring—toiletries, charging cables, snacks, pens, first aid items, tent stakes, you name it. A set of four comes with 2.4L, 1.7L, 1L, and 0.6L sizes and in a variety of fun colors. There’s rarely a trip where at least a couple of them don’t make it into my bag.

Dirty laundry stinks. Literally. That’s why I always pack a lightweight dry bag when I’m traveling and camping. Dry bags are the MVPs of kayaking and river rafting trips, keeping clothes and gear from getting wet. But they’re also my secret hack for stashing stinky clothes until I get home and can wash them. Sea to Summit makes some of my favorite durable bags, but honestly, any roll-top or drawstring stuffsack or dry bag will do the trick when it comes to sealing in the funk.

If you’re like me and refuse to pay a premium for caffeine on the go (hard pass on that mediocre-at-best $7 airport latte), let me introduce you to my go-to backpacking coffee. I tuck a few of these Alpine Start instant coffee packets into my bag on every trip. I’ve made it a habit to pack a leak-proof travel mug (my favorite is Ocean Bottle) and ask for some hot water from an airport café or flight attendant. Flavors include the classic, dirty chai, matcha, and select seasonals. Plus, they taste much better than anything on the beverage cart. Trust me. I’m a self-proclaimed coffee snob.

Hotel pillows are so hit or miss. Sometimes I get lucky with a fluffy, comfy place to rest my head. Other times I’m stuck with a flat or lumpy excuse for a pillow. You know the pain. I’ve started bringing my HEST Camp Pillow along so I can rest assured I’ll get a good night’s sleep, whether I’m in a tent, a hotel room, or 30,000 feet in the air. It comes in small, medium, and large sizes; the small is best for quick trips, the medium is worth the extra squeeze if you’re staying somewhere multiple nights in a row, and the large is my go-to for car camping. If you prefer a neck pillow on flights, the Hest Pro Travel Pillow will ruin all other neck pillows for you.

Most bags are built for one kind of trip. The Thule Aion Duffel is built for all of them. It has been my go-to bag for more than four years on everything from car camping weekends at state parks to international flights to Japan, Copenhagen, and Mexico. Its features make sense for both time outdoors and work trips in the air: The 35L capacity easily fits a weekend’s worth of clothes and then some, and an internal divider splits the duffel into two main compartments, with a padded laptop sleeve sandwiched in between. There’s also a TPU-lined, zippered compartment that locks in odors, moisture, and dirt from hiking boots and swimsuits.

I try to stay off my phone when I’m camping, so I rarely bring a heavy-duty power bank with me. And when I travel, I don’t often need one either since I’m never far from an outlet on a seatback or airport lounge chair. Rather than lugging around a bulky battery pack, I bring the lightweight NESTOUT 5,000mAh power bank in my bag. This little stick of energy gives my electronics (phone and headphones mainly) all the juice I need on the trail and in transit. Its 5,000mAh capacity gives my phone roughly one full charge, and its 15W output tops it off quickly if I need extra power. It’s also fully waterproof, dustproof, and shockproof.

I’ve lost count of how many times a cheap travel-sized shampoo bottle exploded in my luggage on flights and camping trips. Last year I finally invested in some reusable liquid bottles and now I no longer have to worry about a messy surprise when I unpack. Humangear’s GoToob Squeeze Bottles are made of soft, flexible silicone with a no-drip valve and a locking cap. I fill them with shampoo, conditioner, body wash, sunscreen, and even toothpaste. The wide mouth makes them easy to fill and clean, and the TSA-friendly sizes (1.7 ounces for short trips, 2.5 ounces for longer ones) always clear security.

According to recent reports, my favorite shoe for camping, traveling, and just about everything in between is the Arc’teryx Kragg. They’re super comfortable, low-key stylish, and versatile enough to wear on the trail, around town, or on the plane. Originally designed as an approach shoe for climbers with a grippy outsole, the Kragg’s slip-on upper works wonders for a midnight bathroom run at the campsite or breezing through airport security. I love that you can collapse the heel and wear them like slippers on a long-haul flight, which has saved my feet on more than one red-eye. On work trips, they even look sleek enough to wear to dinner (as long as I’m not wearing the pair that’s scuffed up from season after season of camping). Pricey? Yes. Worth the investment? 100 percent.

With a Wildfire Burning Nearby, Shenandoah National Park is Cracking Down on Campfires

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Joern Siegroth / Getty Images).

As firefighters continue to battle a nearby blaze, Shenandoah National Park is implementing rigid fire restrictions due to exceptionally dry conditions and heightened wildfire risks going into Thanksgiving week.

In a Facebook post park officials explained: “These restrictions protect public safety given the elevated risk of wildland fires throughout the park. Shenandoah National Park, Skyline Drive and other facilities and services remain open as scheduled.”.

Under these fresh restrictions, visitors to the area will have to rethink their cooking looks since they are temporarily unable to build, attend, or maintain open fires anywhere within the park’s boundaries, including in established pits, grates, and in grills. These regulations also apply to picnic areas, shelters, and huts in the park.

These rules also impact backpackers who rely on portable stoves while recreating in the area. Liquid and wood-fuel camp stoves cannot be used within the park until further notice. At the moment, campers can still use canister stoves like Jet Boils and MSR Pocket Rockets.

It has been revealed that this announcement came just one day after the White Oak Flat Fire erupted on U.S. Forest Service land about 50 miles southwest of Shenandoah National Park. Since Friday, the fire has grown to 1,800 acres, with 49% containment. So far, 131 wildland personnel have responded to the fire including handcrews, wildland engines, bulldozers and two helicopters. Wildland firefighters are using active suppression strategies to contain the fire. No evacuations have been reported, and a cause for the fire has yet to be released.

The NPS identifies two primary wildfire seasons in Shenandoah that run from February to May and October through December. Wildfires are relatively common in Virginia during the month of November although the frequency and impacted acreage vary by season and seasonal driving factors like low humidity and breezy weather.

Shenandoah park officials expect these restrictions to remain in place until the region receives enough precipitation to reduce fire risks.

Sources indicate that in this economy, climbers can’t afford to pass up a good deal. Unless you’re crafty and have a sewing machine—not to mention a home welding kit—we imagine there are a few things you could use. Most of the deals we outline below can be found at Backcountry, at REI, and at specific manufacturers like Black Diamond.

In a recent development, backcountry launched its Black Friday Sale early on November 20, with deals up to 60% off. We found some of the best deals on climbing shoes there. Competing outdoor retailer REI launched a Holiday Sale on November 13 with up to 25% off discounts that we expect to endure through Cyber Monday. However, if you’re shopping in person, keep in mind that the co-op is closed on Black Friday itself for its annual #OptOutside campaign.

On the brand side, Black Diamond has been running an outlet sale more or less all month with up to 50% off past styles (mostly apparel, but some hardgoods). Black Diamond is offering a Holiday Sale through November 30 with up to 25% off. On November 27, it shifts into deeper Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals of up to 60% off. We found some steals on editor-recommended gear at BD you won’t want to miss.

As you head into the discount madness, here are a couple Black Friday/Cyber Monday shopping tips for climbers:.

Looking to build out your climbing shoe quiver? Is your go-to pair beyond the point of resole or repair? Ready to graduate to a more performance-oriented design? This is your moment. You may be thinking: But I’m not going to be climbing much for the next few months. I’ll just wait.

Industry observers note that real ones know that would be a grave error. Come February or March, you will still need new shoes. But chance are, they’ll be full price. Plus, if you plan ahead and invest now, you can spend the winter breaking them in around the gym. Here are a few standout Black Friday climbing deals on rock and approach shoes to consider below.

If your footwork repertoire involves pockets and micro edging, the La Sportiva Miura VS Climbing Shoe is among the best. Last year, we chose the Miura VS as the best tech shoe out there. With an aggressive downturn and semi-stiff, low-profile toe box, this shoe is perfect for precision climbing up slab and narrow cracks. Note that VS means this shoe uses a Velcro closure.

La Sportiva’s Katana is an awesome technical shoe for edging and beyond. Note that the men’s version is stiffer than the women’s version. This shoe is great for precision placements on slab, narrow cracks, and steep routes. After a buddy gifted me his slightly too small Katanas, I had them resoled and have been loving them indoors and out. You can also check out our review of the Katana here.

With great grip and breathability, these approach shoes strike a near-perfect balance between nimble hiking and climbing performance—without the weight. That’s why we selected the TX2 Evo as our top pick for a lightweight approach shoe last year. We also love that La Sportiva crafts this pair with recycled materials and a sole designed for easy repairs. This is one of the best Black Friday climbing deals out there if you need a good approach shoe.

Industry observers note that we haven’t seen deals this pervasive on shoes in a while. All but ONE of the dozen pairs we gave top billing in our Fall 2026 Shoe Guide are marked down right now at Backcountry. (The only shoe that evaded discounts is the Scarpa Furia Air, our top pick for a “soft/high-feedback” shoe.) You can read our testers’ thoughts on each shoe in our guide, and see the deals on each shoe and what it’s best for below.

The Red Chili Voltage: “a sleeper classic—a tautly crafted, downturned, asymmetrical performance sport shoe with a solid crossover into bouldering.”.

Scarpa VSR LV: “Across a range of styles and grades, testers praised the shoe’s precision on tiny footholds and its power on steep terrain.”.

La Sportiva Ondra Comp: “Maybe the best toe-hooking shoe I have encountered—ever.”.

Mad Rock D2 One: “… I can safely call these the most versatile, ideal for both bouldering and sport.”.

Butora Ibex: “Hardcore boarders, boulderers, and comp climbers will love it, though I also found it versatile for vertical edging.”.

Evolv Phantom Pro: “… offers significant-time driving and grabbing power paired with a velvety, forgiving footbed and single-strap, sock-like closure.”.

Ocún Jett S: “For a ‘narrow’ slipper, the Jett S still has enough lateral stretch to accommodate wide feet, with a comfy last great for long gym sessions—both bouldering and sport.”.

La Sportiva Mantra: “With a major downcamber and mild asymmetry, the sensitive and pared-down Mantra is great for grabbing big, smeary holds.”.

Evolv Zenist Pro: “The Zenist Pro stands out for its edging and all-around prowess, and is perhaps not as smeary or grabby as the marketing would have you believe.”.

Scarpa Generator Mid: ““The Generator Mid’s massive toe box was adept at rand smearing in a sustained corner crack and for the wide stuff, but boxy and insensitive in thin jams.”.

Scarpa Blackbird: “Over months of testing, the Blackbird has certainly lived up to its hype and its price … The edging power on the Blackbird is off the charts, with the best support and stability on square-cut edges of any shoe I’ve worn.”.

Beyond shoes, there’s a lot more climbing gear on sale out there during Black Friday. Ropes, hardware, and more are all marked down 20% or more. Here are our top editor-tested picks.

Most climbers care about the planet. We can do our part in a lot of ways, one of which is buying more planet-friendly gear. Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. This is the first synthetic rope of its kind that relies less heavily on fossil fuels. Of course, the rope has to work, too, and in tests, we found it held up well. It feeds well and proved kink-resistant in our tests. We dubbed it the best eco-friendly cord in our 2025 rope guide.

We tested Mammut’s Alpine Core Protect Rope and called it one of the safest ropes we’d ever used. It also held up remarkably well after significant abuse in the field. By weaving burly aramid fibers into its core, this innovative rope from Mammut helps resist cutting. And right now, you can snag it at 20% off.

Using the same cam-assisted blocking that makes the Grigri the safer choice over an ATC or other devices, the NEOX innovates with an integrated wheel that makes feeding out slack when lead belaying faster and smoother. Petzl also engineered the NEOX with recycled materials to reduce its environmental impact. We’ve used it for rock, gym, and ice climbing and we’re big fans.

Sources indicate that I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air. The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack.

Sources indicate that A chance to save on cams? We’ll take it. Snag one (or a few) of this Black Diamond #.5 to enhance your rack for fast and light missions.

Industry observers note that our top all-around harness of Fall 2026, the Solution uses what Black Diamond dubs Contour Edge Technology for the waist and leg loops, meaning they’re more rigid in the middle, but flexible and soft at the edges for increased comfort. One of our testers found that this made for a climbing harness with “fantastic” hip support. It didn’t cause any uncomfortable pressure or distracting pain points on his body, steadfastly supporting him during 10-hour days on the wall.

One of our editors’ favorite gifts for this holiday season, Trango’s REAL Chalk is better for humans and the planet. This seawater-sourced chalk comes in 50g, 250g, or 500g bags. Makes for a great stocking stuffer—or stock up for yourself for 2027.

It has been revealed that I bought a BD Momentum Full-Body Harness in 2018 or 2019 and am still using it today. It’s been through years of indoor and outdoor climbing with both of my kids. It’s user-friendly, too—a four-year-old can handle putting it on themselves. When my son finally outgrows his next spring, it’s in good enough shape that we will pass it down to another climbing family. This is a great time to save on a kids’ harness that will last until your kid outgrows it.

Perhaps the most hyped carabiner of 2026 (if there is such a thing as carabiner hype), the Magnetron returned by popular demand a few months ago. After quickly going out of stock, what’s been billed as “Alex Honnold’s favorite carabiner” is now back in inventory—and on sale. The biggest boon of this cult-favorite gear is that you can never forget to lock it, thanks to an automatic magnetic locking mechanism. However, it’s not great for ice/alpine climbing and can be a tad difficult to operate for smaller hand sizes. I personally have a small hand and find it easy to use and love it. But you can read our full thoughts here.

It has been revealed that one of our top ice tool picks this winter, the Black Diamond Hydras offer an impeccably balanced swing, ultra-precise pick, and a high degree of modularity make the Black Diamond Hydra our tool of choice for moderate and vertical ice. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

Recent findings suggest that our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

Recent findings suggest that after quickly burning through Black Diamond Crack Gloves (that broke within a few months while climbing an indoor crack), I ordered a pair of these Ocún gloves a couple years ago and have loved them ever since. They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded. (Photo: Michelle Polizzi).

While thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains. Western Appalachia is a hiker’s paradise, with hundreds of miles of trails, accessing some of the Bluegrass State’s most striking landscapes—and the Red River Gorge is one of its crown jewels.

This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky. The powerful Red River carved the Gorge millions of years ago, creating an outdoor playground of cliffs, creeks, waterfalls, and sculpted rock. It has more than 60 official hiking trails and more sandstone arches than anywhere else in the eastern U.S.

Here’s what to see, where to hike, and how to play if you’ve just got one weekend in Kentucky’s Red River Gorge.

Every first-time visitor to the Red River Gorge must visit Gray’s Arch—no exceptions. This massive natural sandstone structure will give you a crash course in the area’s unique topography, including a diverse hardwood forest, massive rock outcroppings, and steep staircases built directly into the hillsides.

While most visitors stick to the 2.5-mile out-and-back trail to Gray’s Arch before turning around, it’s worth extending your hike to 5.8 miles on the Gray’s Arch Long Loop Trail. This route takes you past the crowds that gather beneath Gray’s Arch. It winds deeper into the canyon, through the cool, damp forest, over creeks, and beneath looming rock overhangs that still hold Indigenous petroglyphs.

Whittleton Campground has a free day-use lot with a trailhead accessing multiple hikes. Two trails lead to the Whittleton Arch, and another goes to Hensen’s Arch. Try the standard USFS Whittleton Trail, a 2-mile loop that starts and ends at the campground. Or take the longer Whittleton Branch Trail #216. This 4.8-mile out-and-back accesses the arch and follows a creek for most of its length.

According to recent reports, from the campground, you can also hike the Hensen’s Arch Trail. In less than a mile, you’ll reach a second sandstone arch and a deep sinkhole where you can descend into the Earth via a set of metal stairs.

Sources indicate that if you’re still feeling adventurous after you hike, head to SUP Kentucky for a Crystal Kayak and SUP Glow Tour, where you’ll paddle underground into a submerged former limestone mine. Thanks to limestone’s natural filtration properties, the water is astoundingly clear. Watch schools of rainbow trout swim beneath your LED-illuminated translucent kayaks, as colors refract upon the ceiling.

The highlight of Kentucky’s Natural Bridge State Resort Park is the massive natural bridge (for which it’s named). This impressive geologic feature stands 65 feet high and 78 feet in length.

Recent findings suggest that there are several ways to access the arch. Hikers can take the 5.5-mile Natural Bridge and Battleship Rock Trail, which winds past five different trail shelters. Hikers walk beneath some of the country’s tallest tulip poplar trees—some standing more than 150 feet. Natural Bridge is the trail’s climax. You can view the rock formation from numerous vantage points, and even walk across the arch to the lookout point.

Sources indicate that for a longer, more challenging approach, try the 7.5-mile Sand Gap Trail. It can be done as an out-and-back, or connected with Natural Bridge Trail to make a loop.

Recent findings suggest that for more ridge, arch, and canyon trails, head 30 minutes north of the Natural Bridge State Resort Park to the Auxier Ridge Trailhead. From this hub, hikers can access the 6.0-mile Double Arch Loop, which follows Auxier Ridge and passes Courthouse Rock, Haystack Rock, Double Arch, and Arch of Triumph.

Industry observers note that the Star Gap and Skyview Arch Trail also starts at the Auxier Ridge trailhead. This roughly 6-mile out-and-back hike is narrow and woodsy. It includes some overgrown sections and short scrambles with about 1,300 feet of elevation gain. But the effort is rewarded with access to Skyview Arch at the end.

Dispersed camping is allowed around Auxier Ridge. Or check out the Sandstone Drifter, a reservable cliffside treehouse accessed by a suspension bridge. But be warned: climbing its 177-stair floating staircase is a short, steep hike in itself.

Sources indicate that when rock-climbing traffic slows in winter and early spring, the Muir Valley Nature Preserve is a perfect place to see waterfalls at their full splendor. That’s when precipitation is highest, meaning larger, fuller falls and a chance to see giant icicles and frozen cascades of water. A $15 parking fee is required, and visitors must sign a waiver before entering.

Recent findings suggest that connect Horseshoe Falls, Joe Ponder Falls, Stadium Wall, and Nellie’s Falls to create a moderate, 4.4-mile hiking loop that spans three waterfalls and winds beneath sandstone overhangs. To extend the hike, add Liz’s Arch and Washboard Wall Trail for an additional 1.5 miles, exposing hikers to more arches, cliffs, and several rock-climbing areas.

The underside is coated in a thick, waterproof material that keeps moisture and dirt from seeping through. You can also toss it in your tent to make a cozier floor or dress up your campsite with an outdoor rug.

Good luck wrapping a kayak (or fitting it in your garage). Skip the bulky gift for the packable and portable inflatable ISLE Switch 3. This hybrid SUP-kayak fits in a backpack with everything you need to hit the water, including a paddle, pump, and inflatable kayak seats. It’s the perfect adventure gift for a family who loves getting out on the water.

Keep it old school with this point-and-shoot camera that’s perfectly nostalgic. Don’t let its lack of a screen fool you. It also offers several built-in filters—standard, vintage, analog, and black-and-white—that you can swap with the push of a button. In a recent development, if you want to take the littlest adventures with all their gear along, this wagon makes it easy. It works three ways: as a wagon for hauling, as a stroller with two 5-point safety harness seats, and as a car seat carrier with the included adapter (car seat not included).

The Wrangler Deluxe holds up to 110 pounds and brings the tough, trail-ready spirit Jeep is known for, with all-terrain puncture-proof airless tires and swivel front wheels for easy maneuvering. A removable cooler bag holds up to 16 cans, and the wagon also has a UV-blocking canopy, pull-down shades, a cup holder, a parent organizer, and multiple storage pockets. When it’s time to pack up, it folds compactly.

Cozy up around the campfire with the ones you love in this two-seater camp chair. Its low-profile, reclined design puts you at just the right height for roasting s’mores and soaking up the fire’s warmth. And for a chair that fits two (or three if you’ve got a kiddo on your lap), it packs down surprisingly small.

We can’t mention s’mores without plugging our favorite roasting sticks. These reusable, telescoping metal roasting forks make great stocking stuffers. It has been revealed that due for a new family cooler? Keep beers, bubbly water, juice boxes, and everything in between ice-cold in the Hydro Flask 15L Carryout Soft Cooler.
